figures.shows: Three flowcharts of QGRAND. (a) Syndrome used only as a membership test: state |X> goes to a syndrome check; s = 0 accepts, s not 0 applies the next recovery R_i and loops, and running out of patterns gives correction failed. (b) Syndrome used as an aid: compute syndromes for the stored set N_P, check stored error matches (zero syndrome accepts, one match applies E_i), otherwise iteratively check the N_J errors; no match gives correction failed. (c) General form: preprocessing U, operations W_j, a membership test that passes or fails with information I_i, and an iterative recovery loop that can quit with correction failed.

papers.what_it_is: A 2023 IEEE-format preprint that proposes quantum GRAND (QGRAND), a noise-guessing decoder for quantum random linear codes built from random Clifford circuits, and assesses it by semi-analytical simulation of a Pauli noise channel.

existing.note: The abstract says it, but the body shows it only by semi-analytical simulation (random codes, 31 or 2000 samples), for the stated noise model (Pauli channel, Bernoulli noise), with perfect encoding, perfect measurements and all-to-all connectivity. No theorem proves it for the quantum case. The paper says its codes are near-capacity achieving, with the capacity tied to the hashing bound.
existing.value: The authors state in the abstract that the paper shows it is possible to both construct and decode QECCs that attain the maximum performance of the finite blocklength regime, for any chosen code length when the code rate is sufficiently high. In the body, they say the stabilizer codes are shown, via semi-analytical simulation, to be near-capacity achieving, in a system model with perfect encoding and perfect measurements.
quotes: This paper shows that it is possible to both construct and decode QECCs that can attain the maximum performance of the finite blocklength regime, for any chosen code length when the code rate is sufficiently high.
stabilizer codes that are shown, via semi-analytical simulation, to be near-capacity achieving and decodable in practice
Our work considers a system model with perfect encoding and perfect measurements
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from simulation in one study; the body scopes the abstract's wording to semi-analytical simulation.
existing.reader_inference: The abstract's wording is stronger than the body's, which says near-capacity achieving and rests on simulation and on the cited hashing-bound argument, not on a proof for the quantum case.

existing.note: Section I-B (p.3) adds that the model also has noiseless encoding circuits, noiseless syndrome extraction, noiseless gates and all-to-all connectivity; these are entered as new assertions.
existing.certainty_reason: Section VIII, p.12 to p.13, states the paper's own scope and what it leaves out.
Section VIII, p.13, states it as ongoing work.
An empirical result from simulation in one study (Section V-C, Figure 3).

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that, by combining QRLCs and a newly proposed quantum-GRAND, the work shows it is possible to decode QECCs that are easy to adapt to changing conditions.
quotes: By combining QRLCs and a newly proposed quantum-GRAND, this work shows that it is possible to decode QECCs that are easy to adapt to changing conditions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim; the body argues adaptability in Section VI-D without a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that GRAND is a universal decoder for any block code of moderate length or high code rate with low entropy noise, that its only requirement is a practical membership test, and that its decoding complexity is measured by the average number of membership tests needed until a valid codeword is found.
quotes: GRAND is a universal decoder, enabling the decoding of any block code of moderate length
The only requirement is that a practical membership test exists
The decoding complexity is measured by the average
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result about classical GRAND (references 31 to 36).

assertions.value: The authors state that GRAND does the decoding on-the-fly, dispensing any type of storage besides the parity-check matrix of the RLC, unlike information set decoding, syndrome decoding or trellis-based decoding.
quotes: GRAND does the decoding on-the-fly, dispensing
any type of storage besides the parity-check matrix of the RLC
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim about classical GRAND attributed to the GRAND literature.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 37, that GRAND can outperform information set decoding, syndrome decoding and trellis-based decoding (designed for memoryless channels) when the noise is non-independent and non-identically distributed and has memory.
quotes: Additionally, GRAND can out-
in the case of non-independent and non-identically distributed
noise having memory [37].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 45, that for codewords with n qubits and all-to-all connectivity, a number of two-qubit random Clifford gates of order n log squared n, with circuit depth of order log cubed n, has been shown to lead to codes with a reasonable Hamming distance.
quotes: O n log2 n two-qubit random Clifford gates and O log3(n) circuit depth has been shown to lead to codes with a reasonable Hamming distance [45].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from another paper, with the exponents printed flat in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that their model considers all-to-all qubit connectivity, noiseless encoding circuits, a noiseless syndrome extraction procedure and noiseless quantum gates, and that these are limitations from a practical perspective.
quotes: We note that, from a practical perspective, our model has some limitations.
We consider allto-all qubit connectivity, noiseless encoding circuits, as well as a noiseless syndrome extraction procedure. We also consider noiseless quantum gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I-B, p.3, states the model's limits in the paper's own words.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to their best knowledge, only recently has a practical decoding technique for random-Clifford-circuit codes been presented in reference 46, based on tensor networks and applicable specifically to low-depth circuits with one-dimensional connectivity, and that reference 46 numerically verifies that its code reaches the hashing bound without a mathematical proof.
quotes: only recently has been presented in [46] a practical decoding technique, based on tensor networks, applicable specifically to low-depth circuits with one-dimensional connectivity.
They numerically verify that their code reaches the hashing bound [47], but do not prove it mathematically.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main contributions of the paper are an analysis of the requirements for the construction of a good QRLC, including the implications for encoding complexity measured by the number of gates in the encoding circuit, and a quantum-GRAND approach that enables the numerical assessment of QRLC performance for the first time, with the distance from the analytically derived optimal performance measured.
quotes: the main contributions of the paper are i) the analysis of the requirements for the construction of a good QRLC, including the implications to the associated encoding complexity, measured by the number of gates in the encoding circuit,
the proposal of a quantum-GRAND approach that enables the numerical assessment of the performance of QRLC’s for the first time
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I-B, p.3, is the paper's own statement of its scope and contributions.

assertions.value: The authors define the term error rate in the paper as used in the same sense as bit error rate in classical communications, with respect to qubits after their discretization.
quotes: error rate is used throughout the paper in the same sense that bit error rate is used in classical communications, meaning that herein the term is used with respect to qubits after their discretization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I-C, p.4, defines the term.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing the original GRAND paper, that for noise with Shannon entropy H(N) and code rate R = k/n below capacity (R < 1 - h(N), with h(N) the entropy per bit), the expected number of error patterns to be tested until the true noise pattern is found is, for large n, 2 to the power n times min of h-one-half(N) and 1 - R, where h-one-half is the Renyi entropy of order 1/2 per bit.
quotes: a code rate R = k/n below capacity (i.e., R < 1 − h(N )), the expected number of error patterns needed to be tested until finding the true noise pattern is 2n min {h1/2(N ),1−R}, for large n
where h1/2 is the Renyi entropy of order 1/2 [54], per bit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference 31 (the exponent is printed flat in the text layer).

assertions.value: The authors state that GRAND performs ML decoding, and that GRAND with abandonment (GRANDAB), which stops after slightly more than the first 2nh(N) error patterns (2 to the power n times h(N)), still provides ML decoding and is also capacity-achieving using many fewer iterations.
quotes: GRAND performs ML decoding and can therefore provide capacity-achieving performance
This variant is called GRAND with abandonment (GRANDAB) and still provides ML decoding. In this manner, GRANDAB is also capacity-achieving, using many fewer iterations.
the search may be abandoned after iterating through slightly more than the first 2nh(N ) error patterns
assertions.certainty_reason: A result about classical GRAND attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the GRAND results have been rigorously proven for uniform-at-random codes as n tends to infinity, and that experimental applications using structured linear codes of small blocklength, and RLCs in particular, have produced results consistent with these guarantees.
quotes: Although these results have been rigorously proven for uniform-at-random codes as n → ∞, experimental applications using structured linear codes of small blocklength, and also RLCs in particular, have produced striking results
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the classical GRAND literature.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical use cases such as wired communications or data storage commonly offer error rates below 10 to the power minus 5, while current quantum technologies need to handle much higher error rates, similar to uncoded classical wireless links, between 10 to the power minus 3 and 10 to the power minus 2.
quotes: classical use cases, such as wired communications or data storage, commonly offer error rates below 10−5
similar to the ones encountered in uncoded classical wireless links (between 10−3 and 10−2)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with citations to references 12 and 13 and no measurement in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors list three extra difficulties for QECC construction and decoding: the non-cloning theorem forbids using copies as redundancy, quantum errors are continuous in nature, and any measurement of a state in superposition destroys that superposition.
quotes: the non-cloning theorem shows it is impossible to copy an arbitrary quantum state, thereby forbidding the use of copies as redundancy;
quantum errors are continuous in nature, as the quantum state can be in any superposition of the basis states;
any measurement performed on a state in superposition destroys that superposition, and thus its quantum information is lost.
assertions.certainty_reason: Background attributed to reference 60 and stated by the paper without proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since Y = iXZ, a QECC that can correct X (bit-flip) and Z (phase-flip) errors simultaneously on each qubit can also correct any arbitrary n-qubit error, and, citing reference 60, that a quantum error channel for n qubits may be decomposed as a combination of Pauli strings (a Pauli channel).
quotes: as long as QECCs can correct X (bit-flip) and Z (phase-flip) errors simultaneously and for each qubit, then they can also correct any arbitrary n-qubit error.
it can be shown [60] that a quantum error channel for n qubits may be decomposed as a combination of Pauli strings
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook result the paper states with a citation, not a proof; graded on how the paper states it.

assertions.value: The paper derives that, because error patterns and stabilizers are Pauli strings that commute or anticommute, the conditional application of each stabilizer provides 1 bit of information about the error, so that s stabilizers give an s-bit syndrome that discerns between 2 to the power s error patterns, and a zero syndrome for no error.
quotes: Consequently, the conditional application of each stabilizer provides us with 1 bit of information about the nature of the error.
With s stabilizers, we have a s-bit syndrome, allowing one to discern between S ≜ 2s error patterns
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV, p.5, derives it in equations (5) to (7) from the commute or anticommute property.

assertions.value: The authors state that a random qubit encoding is generated, following the cited work [45], by randomly selecting Clifford unitaries from the two-qubit Clifford group, which has 11 520 elements, and applying each successively to a random pair of qubits among the n qubits, assuming all-to-all connectivity; this assumption is required for the scaling results in [45] and is used in this work.
quotes: There are |C2| = 11 520 such unitaries
This assumption is required for the scaling results in [45], and is used in this work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V, p.5 to p.6, is the paper's own statement of its code construction and assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 45, that as long as of order n log squared n gates are used with circuit depth of order log cubed n, the random construction leads to a highly performant (n, k) code, and that according to reference 16 these complexity orders can be further lowered.
quotes: As shown in [45], as long as O n log2 n gates are used, with a circuit depth of O log3 n , the construction leads to a highly performant (n, k) code, and from [16] it is already known that these complexity orders can be further lowered.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to references 45 and 16.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using results cited from the literature, as long as n > k + H(N), the code is able to correct the error patterns in N with high probability, as a consequence of information-theoretic arguments based on set counting; the result is derived for large n, and similar results apply to lower n.
quotes: n > k + H(N ),
the code is able to correct the error patterns in N with high probability.
This result is derived for large n, but similar results are applicable to lower n
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from cited results (reference 47) and stated for large n without a proof in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a Pauli channel the capacity of stabilizer codes is associated with the hashing bound, that degenerate error patterns can in theory sometimes surpass the hashing bound (references 65 and 66), and that degenerate errors are treated as approximately uncorrectable in the numerical analysis because their effect is negligible in this setting.
quotes: For a Pauli channel, this capacity is associated with the so-called hashing bound
in theory, due to the possibility of degenerate error patterns, it is sometimes possible to surpass the hashing bound [65], [66].
these error patterns are approximately considered to be uncorrectable
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited statement about capacity and the hashing bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ideal approximation, a code that maps each of N error patterns plus the no-error case randomly and i.i.d. uniformly to one of the S syndromes, has no linearity constraint, and that since QRLCs may be thought of as a subset of the codes it can generate, its performance may be considered an upper bound for the QRLCs of interest.
quotes: since QRLCs may be thought of as a subset of the codes that this ideal approximation may generate, its performance may be considered to provide an upper bound for the QRLCs of interest.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument stated without a proof; the paper later observes QRLCs matching the ideal curve.

assertions.value: The authors state that the probability of correcting absolutely all N error patterns, P(f = 1), may be very low while P(f > 1 - epsilon) is still about 1 for epsilon much less than 1, and that their conditions relating n to k, N and epsilon do not assume large n.
quotes: Note that the probability of correcting absolutely all N error patterns P (f = 1) may be very low, while still having P (f > 1 − ϵ) ≃ 1, for ϵ ≪ 1.
Unlike (10), their derivation does not assume large n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V-B, p.7, derives equations (13) to (16) for the ideal random-syndrome code.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to the linearity of the code, the Pauli strings are distributed equally through the syndromes, so that each syndrome has 2 to the power n plus k, equal to S times L, associated Pauli strings.
quotes: Due to the linearity of the code, the strings will be distributed equally through the syndromes
so that each syndrome will have 2n+k = SL associated Pauli strings.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V-B, p.7, follows it from linearity of the code.

assertions.value: The authors state that for two random error patterns E1 and E2 with the same syndrome, the probability that E1E2 is a stabilizer is about 1/L, where L = 2 to the power 2k is the total number of logical operators, so a degenerate code is unlikely for moderate or high k.
assertions.anchor: Section V-B, p.7; Section VII, p.12
quotes: For two random error patterns E1, E2 with the same syndrome, the probability of E1E2 being a stabilizer is ∼ 1/L.
this possibility can be disregarded for moderate or high k.
assertions.certainty_reason: An estimate stated without a full derivation.

assertions.value: The authors report that they sampled 2000 random (16, 1) codes, found that most good codes are non-degenerate with a small percentage degenerate since k = 1 is very low, found that the probability of obtaining a code that corrects all N error patterns decreases quickly with increasing N, and, at the highest shown N/S of 0.025, found P(success) = 0.99 while P(good) is about 0.
quotes: Fig. 2 presents 2000 samples of (16, 1) random codes.
For the highest shown N/S, with N/S = 0.025, P (success) = 0.99, while P (good) ≃ 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 2: for (16, 1) codes at maximum noise entropy, the probability of a good code and of a non-degenerate good code both start at about 1 at N/S = 0 and fall to about 0 by N/S of about 0.02, the degenerate probability peaks at about 0.1 near N/S of about 0.008, and the probability of success stays at about 1 across the range; the theoretical approximations (dots) lie on the observed curves.
quotes: Figure 2. Probability of obtaining a “good” code (blue), that corrects all N error patterns, vs. the ratio N/S, for a (16, 1) code, for the maximum noise entropy case.
which closely match the observed behavior.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as an example noise model, quantum errors form a Bernoulli process in which each qubit suffers an error with probability p, the error is of type X, Y or Z (depolarizing noise), and the error types are identical and independently distributed for each qubit.
quotes: each individual qubit having a probability p of suffering an error. The error can be of type X, Y, or Z (i.e., depolarizing noise), and the error types are identical and independently distributed (i.i.d.) for each qubit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V-B1, p.7, states the paper's noise model.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the Bernoulli noise model, an error pattern of weight t that has the same syndrome as a lower-weight error pattern cannot be corrected, because lower-weight patterns are always more likely, and that degenerate scenarios are disregarded as negligible for large k.
quotes: it cannot be corrected. Here, the
degenerate scenarios are disregarded, since they are negligible
for large k.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument stated in prose; the equation (23) that follows is not proven in detail.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulations that the minimum number of gates for the code to reach relative deviation delta below 0.02 from the ideal random code is N_min = m n (log2 n) squared, with m about 0.13 to 0.15 for the mean (n, k) code and m about 0.21 when all weight t = 1 error patterns must be correctable, each from 31 QRLC samples per case.
quotes: indicate that this minimum number of gates is given by Nmin. gates = mn log22(n).
for the case where we require that all t = 1 error patterns must be correctable (m ≃ 0.21)
the result of averaging the observed correctable fraction of 31 QRLC samples
eventually reaching (δ < 0.02) those of the ideal random code
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical fit from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the theoretical result in the cited work, that the minimum number of gates scales with order n log squared n, is only proved there for some codes, and that here it is observed experimentally for the mean (n, k) code.
quotes: Although this theoretical result is only proved there for some codes, here we experimentally observe it for the mean (n, k) code
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V-C, p.8, states the scope of the proof in the cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, even for larger quantum codes with n = 128, 1000 C2 Clifford gates should suffice for a very high performance for that rate and code length, and that, since most gates are applied in parallel with depth of order log cubed n, the approach enables high-capacity codes with low-depth quantum circuits.
quotes: even for larger quantum codes with n = 128, 1000 C2 Clifford gates should suffice to ensure that the resulting code has a very high performance for that rate and code length.
this approach enables the creation of high-capacity codes with low-depth quantum circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An extrapolation from simulations in one study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 3: the relative deviation delta from the ideal random code falls from about 0.8 to about 1 at about 10 gates to about 0 as the number of gates grows, and reaches the 0.02 line at more gates for larger codes, at about 100 to about 200 gates for the smallest code in the legend and at about 500 gates for the largest; the minimum number of gates rises about linearly with n (log2 n) squared, to about 1000 gates at about 4500, with fitted slopes labelled about 0.135, about 0.147 and about 0.206.
quotes: Figure 3. (a) Relative deviation δ, for different (n, k) codes and error patterns
number of gates to achieve a relative deviation δ < 0.02, for varying n log22(n).
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by the Gottesman-Knill theorem, stabilizer circuits with n qubits can be simulated using only polynomial in n classical resources, so the stabilizers of a random encoding can be extracted by tracking the starting stabilizers Z_i of the (n - k) ancilla qubits through the encoding U.
quotes: The Gottesman-Knill theorem indicates that stabilizer
circuits with n qubits can be simulated using only O(poly(n)) classical resources
The classical simulation takes these starting stabilizers and modifies them through the encoding U , resulting in the desired minimal
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result (references 62 and 63) applied to the paper's construction.

assertions.value: The authors define QGRAND for stabilizer codes as four steps: generate a random QRLC encoding robust to the noise statistics, determine the stabilizers of the encoding by efficient simulation of the stabilizer circuit, perform syndrome measurement using all the minimal stabilizers, and decode with an iterative noise-guessing recovery procedure like classical GRAND by applying the inverse of the error pattern determined.
quotes: Generate a random QRLC encoding U , robust to the noise statistics N .

Apply decoding using an iterative noise guessing recovery procedure, similar to the one in classical GRAND (Section II-A), by applying the inverse of the error pattern determined to the encoded quantum data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI, p.8 to p.9, defines the QGRAND framework.

assertions.value: The paper derives that, because the encoding and stabilizers are random, each error pattern has probability 1/2 of anticommuting with, and so being detected by, each stabilizer independently, so the average number of stabilizers measured until a nonzero syndrome bit appears is less than 2, about 2 measurements when an error occurred.
quotes: each error pattern has a probability of p = 1/2 of anticommuting (and thereby being detected) by each stabilizer
it will take only ∼ 2 stabilizer measurements, on average, to obtain a nonzero syndrome bit when an error actually occurred.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI-A, p.9, derives it in equations (26) and (27) under the independence assumption it states.

assertions.value: The paper gives the average total number of stabilizer measurements until the trial-and-error procedure completes as C = s + (I - 1) times the average number of stabilizers per nonzero syndrome, which is less than s - 2 + 2I, where I is the average total number of iterations of the procedure.
quotes: the average total number of stabilizer measurements
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI-A, p.9, derives it in equations (26) to (29).

assertions.value: The authors state that a downside of using the syndrome only as a membership test is that error correction and syndrome extraction must be applied physically in the quantum circuit at each iteration, which for error-prone implementations may lead to a costly error correction process, as each application of correction gates adds error to the encoded state.
quotes: A downside of this approach is that the error correction and syndrome extraction must be applied physically in the
this approach may lead to a costly error correction process, as each application of correction gates adds error itself to the encoded state.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI-A, p.9, states the limit of the approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that without abandonment the error correction can fail only when an observed error pattern has the same syndrome as a more likely error pattern (the coset leader chosen is not the error that occurred), and that with abandonment a second source of failure is an unlikely error beyond those one wishes to correct, whose probability is kept low by the choice of n.
quotes: the error correction process can fail solely when an observed error pattern has the same syndrome as an error pattern that was more likely to occur, given the noise statistics.
a second source of failure is the probability that an unlikely error occurs, beyond the errors that one wishes to correct.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI-A, p.9 to p.10, argues it from the decoding rule.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given the random nature of the linear code, it takes on average log2 of N_P bits to identify each of the N_P precomputed error patterns, for at most about 2 N_P bits to store using a binary tree, and that singling out a particular error pattern in N requires on average log2 of (N + 1) stabilizer measurements.
quotes: it takes, on average, log2 NP bits to identify each of the NP error patterns, for a total of at most ∼ 2NP bits to store, using a binary tree.
To single out a particular error pattern in N , we require, on average, log2(N + 1) stabilizer measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: An average-case argument for random codes stated without a full proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that precomputing the syndromes of the N_P error patterns allows a priori checking whether the random linear code distinguishes between all of them, so that other random encodings may be tried until one satisfies the requirements, instead of relying on equation (10).
quotes: we may try other random encodings until we are sure that one satisfies the requirements at hand, instead of relying on (10).
assertions.certainty_reason: A procedure proposed without a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that ordering the stabilizer measurements for maximum information gain results in negligible savings in the average number of measurements needed to determine the error, compared with a random ordering, and that ordering the stabilizers to make a more efficient membership test would also give minimal improvement.
quotes: this costly computation results in negligible savings in the average number of measurements that need to be performed to determine the error (see Appendix A), when compared with a random ordering.
ordering the stabilizers to try and create a more efficient membership test would also result in minimal improvement in performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Supported by an approximate argument and a numerical check in Appendix A, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that when s is much larger than log2 of N plus one, which is greater than H, one may work with a smaller subset of the stabilizers chosen for low weight or ease of implementation, but that this biased sampling may negatively affect performance, and that if the encoding is chosen according to equation (10) one should not have s much larger than H.
quotes: However, this biased sampling may negatively affect performance.
if the encoding is chosen according to (10), then one should not have s ≫ H.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the noise statistics N are central to decoding, QGRAND may be adapted on the fly to a changing noise environment or changing error tolerances, by changing the set of error patterns, and, if that is not sufficient, by undoing the old encoding U and implementing a new encoding U'.
quotes: QGRAND may be adapted on the fly to suit a changing noise environment, or changing error tolerances.
the code can still be quickly adapted by undoing the old encoding U and implementing a new encoding U ′
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a measurement in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QGRAND concept is not limited to stabilizer codes, and describe a general high-level implementation with preprocessing and encoding, data verification by a membership test that may give further information, an iterative correction attempt that should be reversible, and a repeat of verification and correction until recovery succeeds or no feasible attempts remain.
assertions.anchor: Section VI-E, Figure 4(c), p.10 to p.11
quotes: The QGRAND concept is not limited to stabilizer codes.
This verification should be reversible, so that subsequent iterations may undo the effects of failed correction attempts.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal stated without a demonstration beyond stabilizer codes.

assertions.value: The authors derive a lower bound on the fidelity of the corrected state, averaged over the noise distribution, by taking the worst case in which every error except the identity maps the data to an orthogonal state, giving the average fidelity at least 1 minus the BLER, so that 1 minus Fmin is bounded by the block error rate, with a difference from code degeneracy.
quotes: A straightforward lower bound may be obtained by considering the worst-case scenario, where all errors in E (except E0 = I) map the initial quantum data to an orthogonal state, resulting in F = 0 if an error occurs.
1 − Fmin turns out to be further lower bounded by the block error rate (BLER)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII, p.11, derives the bound in equations (31) and (32) from the worst-case assumption it states.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by computing the BLER, their results slightly underestimate the codes' performance for very low values of k, and that the BLER is an upper bound to the infidelity in the quantum setting.
quotes: Nonetheless, by computing the BLER, our results slightly underestimate the codes’ performance for very low values of k.
the block error rate (BLER, which is an upper bound to the infidelity in the quantum setting)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII, p.12, states the limit of the BLER measure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the error probability in quantum communications and quantum computation is typically of order 10 to the power minus 3 to 10 to the power minus 1, and that, to motivate near-future use of QGRAND, they consider error probabilities in this range.
quotes: The error probability associated with quantum communications and quantum computation is typically in the order of 10−3 − 10−1
To motivate the use of QGRAND for near-future
applications, for this work, we consider error probabilities in this range.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII, p.12, states the error probabilities the paper studies.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 12, that for fault-tolerant computation it is estimated that an error probability below about 10 to the power minus 2 would be required.
quotes: For fault-tolerant computation, it is estimated that an error probability below ∼ 10−2 would be required [12].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited estimate from another paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results in the two performance figures are semi-analytical: QRLCs are constructed randomly with the Python package Qiskit and their performance is computed exactly from each code's minimal stabilizers; for n = 128 they use 31 samples for each k at least 90, for n = 32 all k are considered, the number of gates varies for n = 128 and is always 2000 for n = 32, and only error patterns up to the chosen weight t are considered.
quotes: The implementation uses the Python package Qiskit. For n = 128, we compute 31 samples for each k ≥ 90. For n = 32, all k are considered.
it varies for n = 128, and it is always 2000 for n = 32
Only error patterns up to the desired weight t are considered; thus N = Bt as in (22).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII, p.12, states the paper's simulation setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that as the code rate increases the code corrects fewer error patterns, with the error rate approaching the case where no error can be corrected, and that lower code rates plateau for each weight t since the codes can eventually correct all error patterns of that weight.
quotes: As the code rate increases, the code manages to correct fewer and fewer error patterns, with an error rate approaching the case where no error can be corrected.
Lower code rates eventually plateau for each weight t, as the codes can eventually correct all error patterns with that weight.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors report that with too few C2 gates the encoding cannot reach the performance of an ideal random code, but with more gates the observed performance of the QRLCs matches it, qualitatively suggesting that GRAND's results for uniform-at-random codes may apply to quantum random encodings, and that the variance of the code performance decreases with more gates.
quotes: but, as more gates are used, the observed performance of these QRLCs matches it, qualitatively suggesting that GRAND’s results for uniform-at-random codes may be applicable to quantum random encodings.
Note that the variance of the code performance also decreases with an increasing number of gates
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study, described by the authors as qualitative.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 5 (n = 128, p = 10−2, correction up to weight three): at low code rate the BLER plateaus for the largest gate count are about 0.38 for correction up to weight one, about 0.14 up to weight two and about 0.04 up to weight three, and all curves rise toward the uncoded value as R approaches its upper end; the fraction of weight-t patterns corrected falls from about 1 to about 0 at R of about 0.8 to about 0.87 for weight three, at a higher R for weight two, and by R of about 0.97 for weight one; curves with fewer gates lie above (worse BLER) and fall at lower R.
quotes: Figure 5. BLER and correctable error fraction f for QRLCs with n = 128, considering p = 10−2, when trying to correct error patterns of weight up to
Top curves: BLER, with shaded areas marking an 80% confidence interval.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors report, for QRLCs with n = 32, that the BLER behaves similarly for p = 10 to the power minus 2 and p = 10 to the power minus 3, that the lower p gives 2 to 3 orders of magnitude lower error rate, and that the fraction of correctable weight-t error patterns is independent of p.
quotes: with an overall behavior similar for both p = 10−2 and p = 10−3, but the lower p enables 2 to 3 orders of magnitude lower error rate.
This value is independent of p.
Figure 6. BLER and correctable error fraction for QRLCs with n = 32, considering different p values
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study (the caption names t up to 3 while the legend lists t = 4).
assertions.reader_inference: The caption says weights up to t = 3 but the legend lists t = 4 curves; the text does not resolve this.

assertions.value: The authors report that increasing n improves the code's performance, with a lower p observing greater improvements, and that the ideal approximation continues to give a quick and good estimate of QGRAND performance.
quotes: As seen in Fig. 7, increasing n improves the code’s performance, with a lower p observing greater improvements.
continues to provide a quick and good estimate of QGRAND’s performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 7 (R = 0.7, Bernoulli noise): the BLER falls as p falls for all three code lengths; the longest code falls from about 0.05 near p of about 0.014 to about 1e-6 near p of about 3e-4, while the shortest code falls from about 0.15 to about 0.005 over the same range.
quotes: Figure 7. Codes’ performance as a function of the probability p of each qubit
suffering an error for different code lengths n, with R = 0.7. A Bernoulli
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that QGRAND is particularly suitable for codes with short codewords or high code rate, and that this type of error protection seems particularly fit to quantum technologies requiring error correction such as the transmission of quantum entanglement, quantum repeaters, quantum memories and quantum computing.
quotes: QGRAND is particularly suitable for codes with short codewords, or with high code
this type of error protection seems particularly fit to the presently envisaged quantum technologies requiring error correction
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion of the authors, partly attributed to reference 52.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although they focus on all-to-all qubit connectivity, the method can be easily generalized to more restrictive connectivities, for example by limiting the two-qubit gates of the encoding to pairs of qubits with a direct connection, with higher circuit depths and limited stabilizer weight.
quotes: Although we focus on the case of all-to-all qubit connectivity, this method can be easily generalized to more restrictive connectivities.
Employing higher circuit depths to achieve similarly powerful encodings, and limiting the stabilizer weight [16] would enable versatile practical implementations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; Section VIII states that limited connectivity is ongoing work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the quantum setting there may be different forms of abandonment, including stopping stabilizer measurements after a given number of measurements, and that in general they expect the QGRAND approach to be directly amenable to the GRANDAB formalism.
quotes: we may also stop measuring stabilizers after a given number of measurements
In general, we expect the QGRAND approach to be directly amenable to the GRANDAB formalism.
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation of the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that in quantum computation the errors during encoding and decoding may be of the same order of magnitude as those in the intended computations, so an important research question is how robust the whole encoding-decoding chain is to such errors, and that the first step should be assessing the impact of imperfect syndrome measurements on the membership test.
quotes: the errors during the encoding and decoding process themselves may be of the same order of magnitude as those encountered in the intended
The first step should be assessing the impact of imperfect measurements when obtaining the syndrome
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VIII, p.13, states the open problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a random ordering of the s minimal stabilizers it takes on average about log2 of (N + 1) measured stabilizers to identify which error pattern occurred, and about 2 times log2 of (N + 1) if the syndrome is used only as a membership test.
quotes: it will take, on average, measuring ∼ log2(N + 1) stabilizers to identify which specific error pattern in E has occurred.
which takes ∼ 2 log2(N + 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: An average-case argument stated without a full proof.

assertions.value: The paper derives, for large N and s and under an approximation that treats the number of anticommuting error patterns as binomial and then normal with independent stabilizers, that the number of iterations of the highest-information-gain ordering is approximately log2 N - log2 log2 s - 1, and concludes the gains over random ordering are negligible so computing a syndrome table for a decision tree is not justified in practice.
quotes: I ≃ log2 N − log2 log2 s − 1.
Thus, it is not justifiable, in practice, to compute a syndrome table
This bound is not exact as the substitution of the binomial distribution
assertions.certainty_reason: An approximate derivation the authors call a rule of thumb, checked numerically in Figure 9.

assertions.value: The authors report, for random (30, 1) codes with only weight t = 1 error patterns, that at maximal noise entropy the decision tree method requires about the same number of stabilizers, log2 of (N + 1), as the naive random method, that for lower entropy distributions only minor savings are achieved, and that the minimum is reached only in the limit of zero entropy where no errors can occur.
quotes: When all cases are equally likely and the entropy is maximal, the decision tree method will require about the same number of stabilizers, log2(N +1) (black solid line), as the naïve method
For lower entropy distributions, only minor savings can be achieved.
Random (30, 1) codes are used, and only error patterns of weight t = 1 are considered.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 8: the number of stabilizers required rises with noise entropy H(N) toward a maximum of about 6.4 at the largest entropy of about 6.4; the constant distribution starts at about 4.2 at zero entropy, the decaying distribution starts at about 6 at zero entropy and dips to about 5 at entropy of about 1 to about 2, and the minimum line is at about 4.
quotes: Figure 8. Average number of stabilizers required to determine the error that occurred, or if no error occurred at all, for different error distributions, as a
Random (30, 1) codes are used, and only error patterns of weight t = 1 are considered.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors report that a least-squares fit of the expected number of iterations of the decision tree method to I = a log2 N - b log2 log2 s - c gives (a, b, c) = (0.96, 0.91, 0.84), approximately in agreement with equation (35).
quotes: a least squares fit obtains the parameters (a, b, c) = (0.96, 0.91, 0.84), which is approximately
in agreement with (35).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical fit from one numerical study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 9: the expected number of iterations falls stepwise as log2 log2 s rises, starting from about 6, about 9, about 12, about 15, about 19, about 22 and about 25 at the lowest log2 log2 s for the seven values of N from the smallest to the largest, and falling by about 3 to about 4 iterations for each N over the plotted range.

papers.what_it_is: A 2022 arXiv paper from Applied Quantum Computing that applies QAOA, VQE and quantum annealing (D-Wave) to a small ambulance location problem and reports simulator, IBM QPU and D-Wave results with practical lessons.

existing.note: The statement sits in the Section VIII A summary. Section VII C 2 (p.52) shows the optimum solution was found only for the smaller grids and none was found from 16 grid locations upward, that no feasible solutions were obtained for the 5x5 grid, and that reverse annealing gave the actual lowest cost state only for the 4x4 grid and a result close to the ground state for 5x5 and 6x6 (Figure 24 shows the feasible state probability falling from about 0.70 to about 0 as the grid grows from 4 to 25 nodes). The 8x8 statement is about trial runs at the largest embeddable size.
existing.value: The authors report that on the D-Wave Advantage they could investigate problems up to an 8x8 grid size, with no feasible solutions found during their trial runs; the success rate in finding the optimum fell rapidly with grid size, with no solutions obtained for problems involving 16 grid locations and above and no feasible solutions for the 5x5 grid; and by seeding reverse annealing with the best forward-anneal state they obtained the actual lowest cost state for the 4x4 grid and close to the ground state solution for the 5x5 and 6x6 grids with 2 ambulances.
existing.anchor: Section VII C 2, p.52; Section VIII A, p.54

papers.version_note: HTML documentation page, last update 03/28/2002. The page holds only two small logo images (OpenCyc and Cyc ball, site decoration); it holds no figure, plot or table.
sections_read: Argument Positions 1-5 (arg1, arg2, arg3, arg4, arg5)
papers.what_it_is: Cycorp's 2002 documentation of how the Cyc knowledge base indexes each term to the assertions that mention it.

existing.note: The page gives the three-layer scheme (argument position, then predicate, then microtheory) with a count at every layer only for the slots arg1 to arg5. Other slots differ: arg0 has two layers (microtheory, assertions), neg and pos have a count at layer 1 and layer 3 but layer 2 holds forward and backward lists with no count, ist has one layer, and 'other' has one layer. Small terms use a simple list. The page does not say the counts are used to know lookup cost; that is the separate 2009 assertion.
existing.value: The page describes the arg1 to arg5 slots of a term's index as three layers (predicate tree, microtheory tree, assertions), and each of the three layers holds a count of the assertions indexed within it. Other slots have different layer structures, and terms with few assertions use a simple list.
quotes: The indexing occurs in three layers: layer 1 : ( <count> . <pred-tree> ) or NIL <count> is total number of assertions indexed within <pred-tree>
layer 2 : ( <count> . <mt-tree> ) <count> is total number of assertions indexed within <mt-tree>
layer 3 : ( <count> . <assertions> ) <count> is total number of assertions in <assertions>
For terms which have relatively few assertions stated about them, the indexing-structure is in fact just a simple list of all assertions mentioning the term.
existing.certainty_reason: Vendor documentation of its own 2002 design.
existing.reader_inference: A count at each layer would let a caller learn the size of a result set before reading it; the page does not state that use.

assertions.value: The page states that an index-structure for an indexed term has slots arg1, arg2, arg3, arg4, arg5, arg0, neg, pos, ist and other.
assertions.anchor: KB Term Indexing in Cyc (introduction), p.1
quotes: Each index-structure has the following slots: (a) arg1, arg2, arg3, arg4, arg5, arg0
(b) neg, pos These slots are used in indexing non-gafs (rules) involving the term. (c) ist If the term is a microtheory
(d) other This slot is used to index all the "none of the above" uses of the constant.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor description of its own design.

assertions.value: The page states that the purpose of the indexing hanging off terms is to provide pointers from a term to all assertions mentioning it, arranged so that groups of assertions that use a term in a similar fashion are efficiently accessible.
assertions.anchor: KB Term Indexing in Cyc (introduction), p.1
quotes: The purpose of all the indexing hanging off of terms in the KB is to provide pointers in the other direction, from a term to all the assertions mentioning it.
To assist in inference, the indexing is arranged to provide efficient access to groups of assertions which use a term in a similar fashion.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor statement of the purpose of its own design.

assertions.value: The page states that the arg0 slot of a predicate's index covers ground atomic formulas where the predicate is used as the predicate, in two layers: a microtheory tree whose layer 1 holds a count, then a list of assertions with a count.
quotes: The indexing occurs in two layers: layer 1 : ( <count> . <mt-tree> ) or NIL
layer 2 : ( <count> . <assertions> ) <count> is total number of assertions in <assertions>
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor documentation of its own 2002 design.

assertions.value: The page states that the neg slot indexes non-ground-atomic formulas in which a term appears in a negative literal, and the pos slot those in which it appears in a positive literal, in three layers: a microtheory tree with a count, a forward and backward split, and a counted list of assertions.
assertions.anchor: Negative and Positive (neg and pos), p.1
quotes: The NEG slot is used to index those formulas in which the term appears in a negative literal. The POS slot is used to index those formulas in which the term appears in a positive literal.
layer 2 : ( <forward> <backward> ) <forward> is layer 3 indexing of forward assertions <backward> is layer 3 indexing of backward assertions
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor documentation of its own 2002 design.

assertions.value: The page states that for neg and pos indexing there are special cases in which a term other than the predicate is indexed: a non-predicate function in a termOfUnit literal, a collection in an isa literal, and an assertion in an abnormal literal.
assertions.anchor: Negative and Positive (neg and pos), p.1
quotes: (b) If #$Foo is a non-predicate function, then #$Foo is used in a literal of the form ( #$termOfUnit ?varN (#$Foo ... )) in all the assertions indexed via these slots.
(c) If #$Foo is a collection, then #$Foo is used in a literal of the form ( #$isa ?varN #$Foo) in all the formulas indexed via these slots.
(d) If <Foo> is an assertion, then <Foo> is used in a literal of the form ( #$abnormal <whatever> <Foo>) in all the formulas indexed via these slots.
